common_name: Golden Celebration Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Golden Celebration's large, heavy blooms benefit from a bit of afternoon shade in the hottest climates and a sturdy, well-branched framework to support the flower weight.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 1992, Golden Celebration is one of the most celebrated of all English roses, bearing very large, deeply cupped, rich golden-yellow blooms with a strong, warm fragrance often compared to sauternes wine and tea, on a vigorous, arching shrub with glossy, disease-resistant foliage. Its combination of flower size, color saturation, and fragrance made it an instant classic, and it repeat-blooms generously from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading, tolerating heat better than many older yellow rose cultivars.

common_name: Lady Emma Hamilton Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Lady Emma Hamilton's dark reddish-purple new foliage is part of its ornamental appeal and contrasts strikingly with the vivid flower color.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 2005, Lady Emma Hamilton produces vivid orange-red buds opening to peachy-orange, cupped blooms that darken toward the petal edges, carrying a strong, fruity, tea-like fragrance, on a compact, well-branched shrub whose new growth emerges an unusual deep reddish-purple before maturing to green. The combination of saturated warm flower color and dark young foliage gives it strong two-tone appeal, and it repeat-blooms reliably from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

common_name: Teasing Georgia Rose (David Austin English Climbing Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation and support for training, since Teasing Georgia is vigorous enough to be grown as a short climber against a wall, fence, or pillar.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, providing a trellis, pillar, or fence if training the vigorous canes upward. Introduced by David Austin in 1998, Teasing Georgia bears deep yellow buds opening to cupped, rich yellow blooms that soften with age, carrying a strong tea fragrance, on long, arching canes that reach 8 feet or more when trained as a climber, or can be kept pruned as a large freestanding shrub. Its vigor and rich, saturated yellow color have made it one of David Austin's most popular climbing selections, and it repeat-blooms well from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

common_name: Falstaff Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Falstaff's very dark flower color is most intense in cooler weather and can bleach somewhat in the hottest, most intense summer sun.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 1999 and named for the Shakespearean character, Falstaff carries deep velvety crimson-purple blooms that darken further as they age, one of the darkest flower colors among English roses, with a strong old-rose fragrance, on a vigorous, arching shrub. Its dramatic, saturated color makes a bold accent in a mixed border, especially paired with lighter pastel companions, and it repeat-blooms reliably from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.

common_name: Tess of the d'Urbervilles Rose (David Austin English Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Tess of the d'Urbervilles blooms in generous flushes and benefits from regular deadheading to sustain repeat flowering through the season.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood. Introduced by David Austin in 1998 and named for the Thomas Hardy novel, Tess of the d'Urbervilles bears dark crimson-red, rosette-shaped blooms with a strong old-rose fragrance, on a vigorous, well-branched shrub with glossy foliage. Its rich, velvety red color and classic old-rose form and scent have made it a favorite among David Austin's darker-flowered introductions, and it repeat-blooms freely from late spring through frost with routine feeding and deadheading.
